title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Analyse and evaluate a scholarly interpretation by weighing it against alternatives.

title: From analysis to evaluation
body: Analysis opens an interpretation up. Evaluation is the next move: deciding how much weight that interpretation actually deserves, once it is sitting next to the alternatives.

title: What evaluation actually means
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.120-121) define evaluation as 'the practice of assessing the relative value of a factor against that of other factors.' The key word is relative: evaluation only means something once you have more than one interpretation to weigh against each other.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students who have each read the same two interpretations.

{{learner-a}} reads two interpretations of the same event and treats them as equally convincing, since both are published.

{{learner-b}} reads the same two interpretations and weighs them against each other using stated criteria: which uses stronger evidence, and which accounts for more of what is known.

Both had read the interpretations. Only {{learner-b}} had evaluated them.

title: Why relative weighing matters
body: Calling an interpretation 'wrong' is rarely useful. Saying which of two interpretations is better supported, and why, is what evaluation actually asks you to do, and it is a more defensible judgement besides.

instruction: Select a highlighted phrase to see why it matters.

_passage.text: Interpretation A rests on a single case study
_passage._note: A single case is suggestive, but it is a narrower evidence base than a wider sample.

_passage.text: , while Interpretation B draws on a larger, more varied sample
_passage._note: A wider sample does not automatically win, but it does carry more weight unless there is a reason to distrust it.

_passage.text: . On the evidence offered, B currently carries more weight, though a reason to distrust the sample would change that.
_passage._note: Stating the criterion (evidence base) and keeping the judgement open to revision is what makes this an evaluation rather than a preference.

title: Slider
displayTitle: How confident are you in weighing interpretations?
body: Rate how confident you feel about weighing one interpretation against another using stated criteria.
instruction: Drag the slider to make your choice, then select Submit.

_feedback.title: Feedback
_feedback.correct: Good. Try applying this to a real pair of interpretations from your own reading this week.

_incorrect.final: Try the annotated example above again, and notice exactly which criterion made one interpretation stronger.

title: Doing this with your own reading
body: When you meet two interpretations that disagree, name one criterion before you decide between them: strength of evidence, size of sample, or how much of the picture it accounts for. State the criterion, then say which interpretation wins on it.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Think of two sources you have read that disagreed. What criterion would you use to weigh them against each other?
Did you ever treat two sources as equally convincing just because both were published? What would change that now?
